_note: STORIES for the reading pages of the English literacy year (Daily Teaching System Part 12.3). Key `g3` (2026-11-16, read by a US Grade 3 reviewer with the rendered pages, every finding applied): five fables and folktales retold in about 210 words and FOUR numbered paragraphs (`parts[].sentences`, written one by one), one library picture; `message` the central message with the message of another story (`lure`) and a sentence that takes the story too literally (`literal`); `shows` three events that show the message, `notInStory` one that the story does not tell, `how` a sample sentence for the key; five `questions` with the paragraph and the proving sentence; four `ask` sentences with their question and a wrong question about the same paragraph; two `traits` (who, the trait, two wrong traits, the sentence that shows it); `connect` as in info-texts.en.json (the story in four events, four actions with what they lead to, a sample because-sentence); `plain` a sentence that shows no trait, `end` how a character feels at the end; `talk` four open questions for a group talk. Key `g2` (2026-11-16, DRAFT, read by no reviewer): five fables retold in about 140 words and THREE paragraphs (beginning, middle, end); `challenge` three questions with a right answer and two wrong ones (the problem, what the character does, a feeling); `links` three causes with their effects; `lesson` with the lesson of another story and a literal sentence; `shows` two events that show the lesson, `notInStory` one that the story does not tell; `retell` the beginning, the middle and the end in one sentence each; `how` a sample sentence for the key. Key `g1` (2026-11-17; types/_shared/story-g1.js): five short original stories of about 70 words in THREE parts (`parts`: beginning, middle, end; arrays of sentences). `chars` two animal characters (name, kind, library picture; the initials differ and none is N); `place` where the story takes place; `details` four questions (answer, two wrong answers, a sentence starter, the whole answer, the number of the sentence that tells it); `map` the setting and the big event to choose or write; `retell` beginning, middle and end in one sentence each and `words` the word bank; `lesson` the lesson and the lesson of another story; `feel` the two feeling words with their face, `sense` the two sense words with the part of the body and two parts that do not fit; `said` three spoken lines and who says them, `told` three sentences of the narrator; `own` and `next` questions with a sample answer.

g3.title: The Lion and the Mouse

sentences: A lion lay asleep in the shade of a tall tree.
A little mouse ran across the grass and did not look where she was going.
She ran right over the lion's nose.
The lion woke up with a roar and caught her under his huge paw.
"Please let me go," cried the mouse.
"If you spare me, I will help you one day."
The lion laughed.
He asked, "How could a tiny mouse ever help the king of the animals?"
But he was not very hungry, and her promise amused him.
He lifted his paw and let her go.
A few weeks later, the lion walked into a hunter's trap.
A net of thick ropes fell over him.
He pulled and twisted, but the ropes only grew tighter.
He roared so loudly that the whole forest heard him.
Far away, the little mouse knew that voice at once.
She ran to the lion as fast as she could.
Then she began to gnaw at the ropes with her sharp teeth.
One rope after another snapped.
At last the lion shook off the net and stood up.
"You laughed at me once," said the mouse.
"Now you know that even a little friend can be a great help."

message.lure: It is wise to work and save today for the days to come.

g3.title: The Ant and the Grasshopper

sentences: All summer long, a grasshopper sat in the sun and played his fiddle.
He sang and danced from morning to night.
Near him, an ant walked back and forth in the heat.
She carried one grain of wheat after another to her nest.
"Come and sing with me," called the grasshopper.
"I cannot," said the ant.
"I am storing food for the winter, and you should do the same."
The grasshopper laughed at her.
"Winter is far away, and there is plenty to eat today," he said.
So he played on, and the ant went back to her work.
Then the days grew short and cold.
Snow covered the fields, and nothing green was left to eat.
The grasshopper had no food and no warm place to stay.
Hungry and shivering, he dragged himself to the ant's nest.
Inside, the ants were sharing the wheat they had stored.
"Please give me something to eat," begged the grasshopper.
The ant looked at him for a long moment.
She asked, "What did you do all summer?"
The grasshopper answered quietly, "I sang."
The ant gave him a few grains and said, "Next summer, sing a little less and gather a little more."
The grasshopper never forgot that winter.

message.lure: Treat others the way you want to be treated.

g3.title: The Crow and the Pitcher

sentences: It had not rained for many weeks.
The streams were dry, and the fields were brown.
A thirsty crow flew from place to place and looked for water.
Her throat was as dry as dust.
At last she saw a tall pitcher on a garden table.
She flew down to it at once.
There was water in the pitcher, but only a little at the bottom.
The crow pushed her beak in as far as it would go.
She could not reach the water.
She tried to tip the pitcher over, but it was too heavy for her.
The crow was close to giving up.
Then she noticed some pebbles on the garden path.
That gave her an idea.
She picked up a pebble in her beak and dropped it into the pitcher.
The water rose a tiny bit.
She dropped in another pebble, and then another.
Each pebble took up some room at the bottom.
It was slow work, and the sun was hot.
But the crow did not stop.
Pebble by pebble, the water climbed higher and higher.
At last it reached the top of the pitcher.
The crow dipped her beak in and drank until she was no longer thirsty.
Then she flew away, pleased with her clever plan.

message.lure: Treat others the way you want to be treated.
message.literal: Crows like to drink from pitchers.

g3.title: Stone Soup

sentences: A hungry traveler walked into a small village.
He knocked on every door and asked for a little food.
"We have nothing to spare," the villagers said, and they closed their doors.
The traveler smiled.
He filled a big pot with water, set it over a fire in the square, and dropped in a smooth stone.
A woman came out to see what he was doing.
"I am making stone soup," said the traveler.
"It is delicious, but it would be even better with a carrot."
The woman was curious.
She ran home and came back with three carrots.
Soon a small crowd stood around the pot.
"A few potatoes would make it perfect," said the traveler.
A farmer brought potatoes.
Then a boy brought an onion, and a baker brought salt and herbs.
One after another, the villagers added what they had hidden away.
The pot bubbled, and a wonderful smell filled the square.
When the soup was ready, the traveler took out the stone.
There was enough soup for everyone in the village.
They carried out tables and ate together, laughing and talking late into the night.
"What a fine soup, and all from a stone!" said the woman.
The traveler smiled again, put the stone in his pocket, and went on his way.

g3.title: The Fox and the Stork

sentences: A fox invited a stork to dinner.
The stork put on her best feathers and came with a big appetite.
The fox had cooked a thin soup, and he served it in two shallow dishes.
He lapped up his soup in no time.
With a grin he asked, "Isn't it delicious?"
The stork could only dip the tip of her long bill into the dish.
She did not get a single drop.
The fox laughed behind his paw.
The stork stayed polite and thanked him for the evening.
"You must come to dinner at my house next week," she said.
A week later, the fox knocked on the stork's door.
A wonderful smell of fish stew came from the kitchen.
The stork served the stew in two tall jars with narrow necks.
She put her long bill into her jar and ate with pleasure.
"Please help yourself," she said.
The fox could not get his nose into the jar.
He could only lick a little stew from the rim.
His stomach growled all evening.
At the door he hung his head.
"I am sorry I played a trick on you," he said.
The stork smiled and answered, "Now we both know how it feels."

message.lure: When everyone shares a little, there is enough for all.

g2.title: The Tortoise and the Hare

sentences: A hare liked to boast about how fast he could run.
One day he laughed at a tortoise for being so slow.
The tortoise was tired of his teasing.
"Let's have a race," she said.
The hare thought this was the funniest thing he had ever heard.
The race began, and the hare shot ahead.
Soon the tortoise was far behind him.
The hare felt sure that he would win.
"I have time for a nap," he said.
He lay down under a tree and fell asleep.
The tortoise did not stop to rest.
Step by step, she kept walking.
When the hare woke up, the sun was low in the sky.
He ran as fast as he could.
But the tortoise was already crossing the finish line.
All the animals cheered for her.
The hare hung his head.
He never laughed at the tortoise again.

g2.title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf

sentences: A boy looked after the sheep on a hill above his village.
Day after day he sat alone, and he was bored.
One morning he had an idea.
"Wolf! Wolf!" he shouted.
The villagers ran up the hill to help him.
There was no wolf, and the boy laughed at them.
The next day the boy played the same trick.
Again the villagers came running.
Again there was no wolf.
"Don't call us when nothing is wrong," they said angrily.
They walked back down the hill.
That evening a real wolf crept out of the forest.
The boy was terrified.
"Wolf! Wolf! Please help!" he cried.
The villagers heard him, but nobody came.
They thought it was another trick.
The wolf chased the sheep far away.
The boy wished he had told the truth.

g2.title: The Dog and His Reflection

sentences: A dog found a big piece of meat.
It was the best meat he had ever found.
He held it tightly in his mouth and trotted home to eat it in peace.
On the way he had to cross a stream on a narrow bridge.
In the middle of the bridge he looked down.
In the water he saw another dog.
That dog also had a piece of meat in his mouth.
It looked even bigger than his own.
"I want that one too," thought the dog.
He snapped at the dog in the water.
But as he opened his mouth, his own meat fell out.
It dropped into the stream with a splash and floated away.
The other dog was gone, too.
It had only been his own reflection.
The greedy dog went home hungry.

g2.title: The Wind and the Sun

sentences: The wind and the sun argued about who was stronger.
Just then a traveler came down the road in a warm coat.
"Let's have a contest," said the sun.
"Whoever can make him take off his coat is the stronger one."
The wind agreed and went first.
The wind blew as hard as he could.
Leaves flew, and the trees bent low.
But the harder the wind blew, the tighter the traveler held his coat.
At last the wind was out of breath and gave up.
Then it was the sun's turn.
She came out from behind a cloud and shone gently.
The air grew warm, and then hot.
The traveler wiped his face.
Soon he took off his coat and sat down in the shade.
The sun had won without any force at all.

g2.title: Belling the Cat

sentences: The mice in the old barn had a problem.
A cat lived there, and she was quick and quiet.
They never heard her coming.
One night the mice held a meeting.
"We must do something," said the oldest mouse.
A young mouse jumped up.
"I have a plan!" he said.
"Let's tie a bell around the cat's neck. Then we will hear her and run away in time."
All the mice cheered.
They thought it was a wonderful idea.
Then the oldest mouse spoke again.
"It is a clever plan," she said.
"But who will put the bell on the cat?"
The barn grew very quiet.
Nobody wanted to go near the cat.
One by one, the mice slipped back into their holes.
